definition: Visionary means boldly imaginative about what the future could become.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word visionary. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know visionary should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Bankers laughed in 1971 when the visionary economist predicted that shoppers would one day wave a plastic card instead of counting out bills.
Forward-looking credits someone with planning ahead; visionary goes further, crediting them with imagining a future others cannot yet see.
Prophetic outruns visionary: the visionary designer imagines what the future could become, while a prophetic warning turns out to state what the future actually did.

Farsighted credits someone with seeing consequences well ahead — the planner who spots next decade's water shortage in this year's rainfall charts. Visionary goes beyond sight to imagination: boldly picturing a future that follows from no trend line at all. A farsighted budget prepares for what is coming; a visionary sketch invents it.

Pioneering praises being first to actually do a thing — opening the trail, running the first experiment, founding the field. Visionary praises being first to see it: imagining what the future could become, sometimes decades before anyone can build it. A pioneering surgeon performs the new operation; a visionary one describes it a generation early.

Visionary means boldly imaginative about what the future could become.
In 1919, a visionary school superintendent argued that every child would someday need to type, and ordered typewriters for classrooms that still lacked electric light.
The purchase was ridiculed as folly; two generations later it looked like a prophecy filed early.
Visionary praises imagination aimed at the future - seeing what could exist decades before it does.
It differs from fanciful, which imagines freely without caring whether the vision could ever come true.
Visionary is high praise for future-facing imagination that history may prove right.
Its unit-mates split the territory: audacious praises the nerve of a bold move made now, and idealistic describes devotion to principles that may float above the facts.
Call a plan visionary only when its boldness lies in seeing what is coming.

In 1959, agronomist Ruth Okafor addressed a farming congress about the century ahead.
Her colleagues forecast better tractors and hardier wheat; Okafor described farms stacked forty stories high in the middle of cities, watered by their own recycled rain.
Nothing in the data pointed there - no tower farm existed, and no bank would have funded one - so the trade papers ran the speech as a joke.
Historians now call the lecture visionary, less for its details than for imagining a future no trend of the time even gestured toward.
The first commercial tower farm opened fifty-eight years later, closely matching her sketch.
